title: Checkpoint: Art Around the World
objective: After this level you can compare art traditions from Japan, China, Africa, Australia and the Americas.
summary: Prussian blue, invented in Berlin, colored Hokusai's Fuji prints, which Europeans admired as Japanese. Across the chapter, influence flows both ways.

cards.headline: The famous blue of the Great Wave was invented in Berlin.
cards.body: Level 71's wave crashed into Europe in Level 72. But its blue had already made the trip the other way. This checkpoint follows art across borders, in both directions.

cards.fact: The "Japanese" blue that dazzled Europe was European.
cards.context: Prussian blue, the first modern synthetic pigment, was created by accident in Berlin around 1705. By the early 1800s it was made more cheaply in China and reached Japan, where it was called bero, from the Dutch for "Berlin blue". Hokusai used it all through Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, including the Great Wave. Europeans who admired the prints often took that blue for a traditional Japanese color.

mascot.line: Art borrows, then lends it back with interest.

cards.headline: Borrowing goes both ways
cards.body: Look back across the chapter and influence keeps flowing in every direction. Japanese prints showed Degas new ways to frame a scene. African masks changed the faces in Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, while Olowe of Ise's palace door traveled to London. Rivera learned fresco in Italy and Cubism in Europe, then used them to paint The History of Mexico. No tradition here is a footnote to another. Each one is a voice in the conversation.
